commenti.body:
There's some stuff there about impotence or the protagonist's manhood being challenged (feels like the wife conversation is just setting up that he's bad at confrontation), but my hot take is that *Duel* is just an efficiently simple thriller premise that maps easily to whatever interpretations you wanna make. 

I could be totally wrong, and I don't ever wanna discourage these kinds of discussions, but aside from Spielberg being a very young filmmaker with a ton to prove (which seriously shows given how much technique is in every single shot here) this really does primarily feel like a movie about how much it would suck to be chased by a big, scary truck. It's a realistic enough fear pushed to an absurd endpoint, while being so intentionally light on extraneous details that each scene is just about dealing with a present situation.

Which is great! A very young Spielberg made a movie about being chased by a truck as engaging as he possibly could for 90 minutes, then got out as soon as the conflict was over. It's not a movie I'm rushing to analyze because I think the charm of it is that it's so stripped back and austere in its plotting. It doesn't need a complex read to be interesting; if anything it's interesting because it's so beautifully simple.

I've always seen the Truck as an animal, or monster if you will. A bit like Jaws in that respect.

I remember reading they deliberately chose a truck that had facial features, and the noises it makes are almost animal like, particularly at the end where you can hear it roar.

You never see the driver (apart from a brief arm shot) so it is like the truck is driving itself with no human controlling it. The truck also has numerous licence plates on it, which I have always interpreted as previous victims

I concur: This film is mostly just what it is, a wonderful thriller.

Having said that, there are some minor curios to be found.  The protagonist’s name is David Mann, which was a somewhat popular thing to do back then… he’s an “every man”, even in his generic name!  Yes there is also the argument with his wife.

But, again, it felt to me these were underdeveloped curios. The film’s primary purpose is to thrill you!

How awesome to see this film come up for discussion! I’ve had a special fondness for *Duel* since I saw it as a young child and it scared the ever loving bejeebers out of me.

>I wonder how he has changed 

I’ve always felt the final shots of the protagonist, screaming in triumph and exultation then almost immediately sinking into a subdued state (finishing with him dejectedly tossing pebbles into the dust) indicates that he’s distraught, or traumatized, by the experience and the gravity of having killed another human being (though it was entirely in self-defense). I suppose it could also be indicative of the weariness and exhaustion that follows after an adrenaline experience. 

Given this ending, and his earlier brittle state (freaking out in the diner), I think this character is going to have some major PTSD. I’ve always appreciated this as a more true-to-life ending than the usual action film where the protagonists commit murder without a qualm.

Not that it enters into the film discussion at all, but as a side note: Richard Matheson, the author who wrote the short story on which the movie is based, explained that the idea came from an experience he had on the day JFK was assassinated. RM and a friend were driving in the desert and a truck driver came up behind them and, for no reason that they could identify, became very hostile and ran them off the road.

I once had a similar (but ridiculously shrunken-down) experience with a middle-aged woman in a compact car in a 35-mph zone. I was behind her, and she was going about 25 so I switched lanes (2 going the same direction). She immediately sped up, cut in front of me, brake checked me, and then slowed down again. So I changed lanes again and she sped up to like 50. Such randomly hostile behavior out of nowhere is so uncanny and weird. To this day I puzzle about that.

Spielberg spoke about this himself - he just wanted to make a cool thriller about a guy being chased by a truck, but once the film became so successful he was allowed to turn it into a theatrical movie (with extra scenes etc.) it then played in big European festivals and got all these reviews and analyses looking for deeper meanings, and finding quite ingenious ones.

He said it led him to realise that there isn't really any one interpretation of a film that's valid - that different people will see different things and that's OK. Quite an interesting perspective for a filmmaker who's come to be seen as so directly manipulative of an audience.
